abstract.p: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) features a dense desmoplastic stroma dominated by type I collagen, which forms a physical barrier that limits vascular perfusion and drug penetration, resulting in poor therapeutic outcomes. Here, we report gemcitabine-loaded collagenase-conjugated liposomes (GLCLs) that enzymatically remodel the collagen-rich extracellular matrix (ECM) while delivering a cytotoxic payload. GLCL retained enzymatic activity and stability, exhibited prolonged circulation, and achieved superior tumor accumulation with deeper and more homogeneous intratumoral gemcitabine penetration than nonfunctionalized liposomes. In PDAC-bearing mice, GLCL showed a 6-fold higher tumor growth inhibition (69.8%) than gemcitabine-loaded liposomes without collagenase (GLL; 10.9%) at the same dose. Importantly, this work provides the first molecular-level validation of nanocarrier-mediated drug penetration in PDAC, achieved through a multiscale approach combining in vivo imaging, ex vivo fluorescence, and quantitative desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging (DESI-MSI). GLCL enzymatically overcomes PDAC’s fibrotic collagen barrier, offering a clinically translatable strategy for deep intratumoral drug delivery.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal human malignancies and is projected to become one of the top causes of cancer-related deaths by 2030. According to GLOBOCAN (Global Cancer Observatory, IARC) 2022 estimates, approximately 510,992 new PDAC cases and 467,409 related deaths occurred worldwide, yielding a nearly 1:1 incidence-to-mortality ratio that reflects both the intrinsic aggressiveness of the disease and the stagnation in therapeutic progress. , With a 5-year survival rate of less than 9%, PDAC continues to represent a devastating diagnosis and highlights the urgent need for innovative therapeutic strategies. ,

A defining feature of PDAC that contributes substantially to its limited therapeutic efficacy is its pronounced desmoplastic stroma. PDAC tumors develop a dense fibrotic microenvironment that can occupy the majority of the tumor mass. , This fibrotic microenvironment is enriched with activated pancreatic stellate cells and dense extracellular matrix (ECM) components, particularly fibrillar collagens and proteoglycans such as hyaluronan. −
Collagen, dominated by type I fibers, accounts for most of the ECM content in PDAC. , The highly cross-linked collagen network, together with excess hyaluronan, elevates interstitial fluid pressure and compresses tumor vasculature, resulting in a hypovascular milieu with severely restricted drug transport. ,, This “fibrotic fortress” not only hinders penetration and distribution of small molecules but also poses a formidable barrier to nanoparticle-based carriers, including liposomes, which despite prolonged circulation time, often fail to achieve deep intratumoral access. Consequently, the collagen-rich stroma is strongly associated with drug resistance and poor clinical outcomes. −

To address these limitations, several strategies have been explored, including modulation of nanoparticle size, enhancement of vascular permeability, and ECM remodeling. −
Among these, enzymatic degradation of fibrillar collagens has attracted sustained attention. −
Collagenases, such as type I collagenase from Clostridium histolyticum, cleave triple-helical collagen fibers into soluble fragments, thereby loosening the dense matrix and reducing stromal rigidity. Preclinical studies in pancreatic tumor models have shown that collagenase administration can reduce stromal density and improve drug uptake. −
However, these studies have almost exclusively relied on surrogate tracers, such as fluorescent probes or histological markers, to infer improved penetration, leaving unresolved whether therapeutic agents themselves achieve enhanced intratumoral delivery. This critical gap has limited the translational impact of ECM-remodeling strategies, as the true therapeutic benefit remains uncertain without direct molecular evidence of drug distribution.

Here, we report the development of gemcitabine-loaded collagenase-conjugated liposomes (GLCL), designed to degrade the collagen-rich ECM while delivering cytotoxic payloads into PDAC tumors. In this platform, gemcitabine is encapsulated in the liposomal core, while collagenase type I is surface-conjugated to enable enzymatic matrix remodeling (Figure b). The optimized GLCL retained structural integrity and enzymatic activity, achieved superior tumor accumulation and deep tissue penetration in vivo, and produced significantly enhanced antitumor efficacy compared with controls. Critically, moving beyond conventional in vivo, ex vivo, and fluorescence microscopic imaging, we employed desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging (DESI-MSI) as an integrated molecular imaging approach to directly visualize and quantify 2′,2′-difluoro-2′-deoxyuridine (dFdU), the principal metabolite of gemcitabine, within PDAC tissues. This multimodal framework provides the first molecular-level evidence that collagenase-functionalized nanocarriers can overcome stromal barriers and achieve deep intratumoral drug penetration. Collectively, these findings establish GLCL as a promising theranostic nanoplatform that not only augments the efficacy of conventional chemotherapy but also enables molecular validation of drug delivery in PDAC.

sec.title: Results and Discussion
Physicochemical Characterization and Stability of GLCL
sec.p: To establish a stable and functionally active nanoplatform capable of enzymatically remodeling the tumor stroma (Figure b), we first optimized the physicochemical parameters of the GLCL in comparison with gemcitabine-loaded liposomes without collagenase (GLL). We systematically tuned the molar ratio between gemcitabine and type I collagenase to preserve colloidal stability while maintaining sufficient enzyme density for ECM degradation. Among the tested ratios, the formulation containing 11 mM gemcitabine and 70 μM collagenase exhibited the most stable hydrodynamic properties over 7 days (Figure a), indicating an optimal balance between drug loading and surface enzyme conjugation. Excessive enzyme conjugation (>80 μM) caused mild aggregation, highlighting the trade-off between biochemical functionality and structural integrity, a key design consideration for circulation-stable enzyme nanocarriers.

caption.p: Physicochemical properties and colloidal stability of GLCL and GLL. (a) PDI stability analysis used to optimize the collagenase-to-gemcitabine molar ratio during GLCL synthesis (n = 3, mean ± SD). (b) Hydrodynamic size distributions of GLCL and GLL measured by DLS (n = 3, mean ± SD). (c, d) Representative TEM images of GLCL and GLL, respectively. (e, f) Time-dependent size and PDI stability of GLCL and GLL in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at room temperature and 37 °C over 7 days (n = 3, mean ± SD). *: P < 0.05.

sec.p: The particle size and morphology analyses further confirmed that GLCL maintained well-defined structural characteristics. The hydrodynamic size of GLCL was 50.77 ± 17 nm with a polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.179, and GLL showed a size of 50.66 ± 16 nm with a PDI of 0.138 (Figure b). The values represent the average of three independent measurements (n = 3; mean ± SD). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis confirmed that the particle sizes were consistent with those measured by dynamic light scattering (DLS) (Figure c, d). In addition, GLCL maintained consistent size and PDI values under both temperature conditions, despite the presence of surface-conjugated collagenase, demonstrating stability comparable to that of the control group GLL (Figure e, f; Figure S1a, b). Furthermore, no visible aggregation or precipitation was observed (Figure S1c).

Collectively, these results demonstrate that GLCL maintains nanoscale uniformity and colloidal stability despite surface enzyme conjugation, providing a robust foundation for subsequent studies on enzyme activity, ECM remodeling, and in vivo penetration.

sec.title: Evaluation of Gemcitabine Encapsulation and Collagenase Surface Functionalization in GLCL
sec.p: After establishing the physicochemical stability of GLCL, we next confirmed that collagenase was successfully conjugated to the liposomal surface while retaining enzymatic activity, a prerequisite for ECM remodeling in desmoplastic pancreatic tumors.

The optimized formulation achieved a gemcitabine loading efficiency (LE) of 15.3% and a collagenase conjugation efficiency of 10.4%, consistent with the desired ratio for balanced drug payload and surface enzyme density (Figure a). To verify the molecular proximity between the liposomal bilayer and surface-bound enzyme, Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) analysis was performed using FITC (donor)–Nile Red (acceptor) pairs. , Effective binding of collagenase to the liposomal surface induced FRET, as evidenced by FITC fluorescence quenching accompanied by an increase in Nile red emission. The maximum emission wavelengths (λem) were observed at approximately 520 and 635 nm, corresponding to FITC and Nile red, respectively. A high FRET efficiency of 78.7% and an estimated donor–acceptor distance of 4.7 nm confirmed that collagenase was covalently anchored to the liposomal surface rather than loosely adsorbed, ensuring stable enzyme presentation under physiological conditions (Figure b). The measured high FRET efficiency and the calculated distance fall within the optimal range for efficient energy transfer, supporting the close proximity between the donor and acceptor fluorophores. These findings are consistent with previous reports demonstrating successful surface conjugation via FRET. −

caption.p: Detailed evaluation of gemcitabine incorporation and collagenase type I functionality in GLCL. (a) Gemcitabine loading efficiency within the hydrophilic core of GLCL (n = 3, mean ± SD). (b) FRET emission spectra to confirm collagenase attachment to GLCL. FRET was performed using three experimental groups: (1) GLCL conjugated with only FITC-labeled collagenase, (2) GLCL loaded with Nile Red and conjugated with FITC-labeled collagenase, and (3) GLCL containing Nile Red only. Nile Red (acceptor, λem = 635 nm) and FITC (donor, λem = 520 nm) (n = 3, mean ± SD). (c) Ninhydrin assay comparing GLCL and free collagenase type I to verify collagenase binding to the surface of GLCL. (d) Stability of enzymatic activity of collagenase type I on the surface of GLCL over 7 days at room temperature and 37 °C (n = 3, mean ± SD).

sec.p: Additionally, a ninhydrin assay was conducted as a supplementary experiment to evaluate collagenase conjugation. Ninhydrin is a well-established reagent that reacts with primary and secondary amines, producing a characteristic blue-purple color. Leveraging this property, we estimated the degree of amino group substitution between free collagenase type I and GLCL by comparing the slopes of their regression lines, thereby inferring the extent of collagenase conjugation on the GLCL surface. Consequently, the slopes for free collagenase and GLCL were determined to be 0.0493 (R 2 = 0.996) and 0.0358 (R 2 = 0.980), respectively. The degree of substitution (%DS), calculated from the difference between these slopes, was approximately 27.4% (Figure c). These results suggest that a substantial portion of the accessible primary amine groups on collagenase were successfully conjugated to the liposomal surface. Collagenase inherently bears multiple primary amines, particularly ε-amines of lysine residues, as demonstrated in classic chemical modification studies identifying essential lysyl residues in C. histolyticum collagenases. , This further justifies the use of the ninhydrin assay for evaluating its conjugation to liposomes.

Finally, to verify that collagenase immobilized on the GLCL surface retained its enzymatic functionality, we evaluated its activity and stability using the EnzChek Gelatinase/Collagenase Assay Kit. GLCL exhibited an enzymatic activity of 0.17 U, compared to 0.4 U for free collagenase (Figure S2b, c). Although surface conjugation led to a reduction in apparent enzymatic activity compared with the free enzyme, collagenase immobilized on the GLCL surface retained measurable and functionally relevant enzymatic activity. Importantly, the stability of collagenase conjugated to the GLCL surface was monitored over 7 days under both room temperature and 37 °C conditions, confirming that enzymatic activity was effectively maintained under both conditions (Figure d). This sustained enzymatic activity supports the potential of GLCL as a stable and functional nanocarrier capable of ECM remodeling, which is particularly relevant for pancreatic tumors characterized by dense stromal collagen that limits drug penetration.

sec.title: Enhanced Cytotoxicity and Cellular Uptake of GLCL Compared to GLL
sec.p: To evaluate whether collagenase conjugation translates into functional advantages at the cellular level, we first compared the cytotoxicity of GLCL and GLL in two cancer cell lines, KPCY 7160c5 (murine PDAC) and Panc-1 (human PDAC).

An MTT assay was conducted to evaluate the cytotoxicity of free gemcitabine in two different cell lines using equivalent gemcitabine concentrations (0 to 2 mg/mL). The resulting IC50 values were 0.549 μg/mL for KPCY 7160c5 cells, 0.086 μg/mL for Panc-1 cells (Figure S3a, b). Subsequently, a comparative evaluation of GLCL and GLL was performed in the same cell lines. In KPCY 7160c5 cells, GLL showed significant cytotoxicity at concentrations of 18.75 μg/mL and above, whereas GLCL induced cytotoxic effects starting at 2.34 μg/mL, demonstrating superior cancer cell-killing efficacy across the 2.34–37.5 μg/mL range compared to GLL (Figure a). In Panc-1 cells, GLL began to exhibit cytotoxicity at 4.69 μg/mL and above, and GLCL also induced cytotoxicity at the same concentration. GLCL demonstrated greater cytotoxic effects than GLL within the 9.38–37.5 μg/mL range (Figure b). Collectively, MTT assays showed that GLCL exerted stronger cytotoxic effects than GLL in PDAC cell lines. This enhanced cytotoxicity of GLCL may be associated with the degradation of cell-derived pericellular ECM by surface-displayed collagenase, thereby facilitating closer proximity between nanoparticles and tumor cells. PDAC cell lines, including Panc-1 and KPC-derived cells, have been reported to express and produce type I collagen, which may contribute to a cell-associated or pericellular collagen-rich microenvironment. ,, To directly visualize this effect, we next compared the time-dependent cellular uptake of DiD-labeled GLCL and GLL using confocal fluorescence imaging.

caption.p: Comparative in vitro cytotoxicity and cellular uptake of GLL and GLCL in KPCY 7160c5 and Panc-1 cells. (a, b) Cell viability analysis following treatment with GLL and GLCL at equivalent gemcitabine concentrations (0–37.5 μg/mL) in KPCY 7160c5 and Panc-1 cells using the MTT assay. Statistical significance was determined using a two-sided Student’s t-test (n = 3, mean ± SD). (c) Representative confocal images showing time-dependent cellular uptake in KPCY 7160c5 cells incubated with the particles for 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h (blue: Hoechst 33342 for nuclei staining; green: ViaFluor 488 for cytoskeleton staining; red: DiD labeling of GLL or GLCL; NS: normal saline; TD: transmitted light channel; scale bar: 75 μm). Quantification of DiD fluorescence intensities at (d) 30 min, (e) 2 h, and (f) 6 h in KPCY 7160c5 cells treated with DiD-labeled GLL and GLCL. Data were statistically analyzed using Student’s t-test (n = 7, mean ± SD). *: P < 0.05, **: P < 0.01, ***: P < 0.001, ****: P < 0.0001.

sec.p: To investigate the mechanism underlying the enhanced cytotoxicity of GLCL, we examined cellular uptake in the representative KPCY 7160c5 cell line, selected as the primary model for subsequent therapeutic studies. DiD-labeled GLCL exhibited significantly greater time-dependent uptake compared to GLL (Figure c). Notably, intracellular fluorescence intensity was markedly higher in GLCL-treated cells at 30 min (P < 0.05), 2 h (P < 0.001), and 6 h (P < 0.0001), confirming more efficient internalization (Figure d–f). These in vitro findings suggest that GLCL’s enzymatic surface activity improves gemcitabine delivery at the cellular interface, resulting in the higher in vitro cytotoxicity and providing a mechanistic basis for the enhanced tumor accumulation observed in subsequent in vivo imaging studies.

sec.title: Enhanced Tumor Accumulation of GLCL Revealed by In Vivo Fluorescence Imaging in KPCY 7160c5 Tumor-Bearing Mice
sec.p: The tumor accumulation and biodistribution of GLCL were evaluated using in vivo and ex vivo fluorescence imaging in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice (Figure a, b). After intravenous administration, in vivo imaging revealed markedly stronger tumor fluorescence in the GLCL-treated group compared with the GLL-treated controls at all observed time points up to 24 h postinjection (Figure a). Subsequent ex vivo imaging of dissected organs confirmed preferential tumor accumulation of GLCL (Figure b). Quantitative ex vivo analysis revealed significantly higher accumulation of GLCL in tumors and liver, with 12.4-fold and 2.8-fold increases in uptake, respectively, compared to GLL (Figure c, d). To minimize potential imaging bias due to different fluorescence intensities of the two nanoparticles, tumor-to-organ fluorescence ratios were calculated, revealing that GLCL exhibited substantially greater tumor selectivity. Specifically, the tumor-to-liver, tumor-to-spleen, and tumor-to-lung ratios were 2.88-, 2.51-, and 1.55-fold higher, respectively, than those of GLL (Figure e–g). These findings corroborate the qualitative imaging data with a more robust and biologically relevant metric, suggesting that collagenase-mediated ECM remodeling reduces stromal barriers, thereby enhancing nanoparticle penetration and selective tumor accumulation, which are critical determinants of therapeutic efficacy in vivo. ,, Quantitative fluorescence levels in the lung, spleen, heart, and kidney, as well as tumor-to-heart and tumor-to-kidney ratios, are shown in Figure S4b–g. Collectively, in vivo and ex vivo imaging consistently demonstrated superior tumor accumulation of GLCL compared to GLL, likely attributed to the effects of enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) and collagenase-mediated ECM remodeling. , This enhanced accumulation is consistent with previously described mechanisms of collagenase-mediated ECM remodeling, which are known to reduce interstitial fluid pressure and loosen the dense fibrotic network characteristic of PDAC, thereby facilitating nanoparticle transport into deeper tumor regions. , These fluorescence biodistribution results provide strong in vivo evidence that GLCL overcomes stromal barriers and achieves superior tumor-targeting efficiency compared with conventional liposomes.

caption.p: In vivo and ex vivo fluorescence imaging to evaluate the biodistribution and tumor accumulation of DiR-labeled GLCL and GLL in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice (n = 5). (a) In vivo fluorescence images of KPCY 7160c5 tumor model mice at 0, 2, 6, 12, and 24 h after intravenous injection of GLCL or GLL (dorsal view: left column; abdominal view: right column). White circles indicate tumor locations. (b) Ex vivo fluorescence images of major organs and tumors. All tissues were resected from mice after in vivo imaging (He: heart, Li: liver, Sp: spleen, Ki: kidney, Lu: lung). Quantitative fluorescence analysis of the (c) tumor and (d) liver (FL intensity, mean ± SD). Tumor targeting efficiency was assessed by comparing tumor-to-organ fluorescence intensity ratios for the (e) liver, (f) spleen, and (g) lung. These ratios were statistically analyzed using Student’s t-test (n = 5, mean ± SD). *: P < 0.05, **: P < 0.01, ****: P < 0.0001.

sec.title: Intratumoral Penetration and Spatial Distribution of GLCL
sec.p: Based on the enhanced tumor accumulation observed in in vivo fluorescence imaging, we next examined whether GLCL could penetrate more deeply into the tumor parenchyma. The distribution of GLCL and GLL within tumors was assessed using dual-fluorescence tracking in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice (Figure a).

caption.p: Comparative intratumoral penetration of GLCL and GLL in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice. (a) Schematic illustration of the tumor penetration test procedure. (b) Confocal images of KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice treated with NS, GLL, or GLCL. Tumors were sectioned through the center. RITC was encapsulated in the hydrophilic core of liposomes to trace gemcitabine distribution, while DiD was incorporated into the hydrophobic lipid bilayer to trace the liposomes (GLCL or GLL). (Blue: liposomes (DiD); Red: gemcitabine (RITC); hot: normalized and subtracted (RITC-DiD), TD: transmitted light channel; scale bar: 1 mm). Quantitative analysis of (c) RITC and (d) DiD fluorescence intensities in tumor tissues. (e) Coefficient of variation (CV) of RITC intensity images indicating fluorescence homogeneity. All data were statistically analyzed using Student’s t-test (n = 3, mean ± SD). *: P < 0.05.

sec.p: As shown in Figure b, tumor sections from the GLCL-treated group exhibited markedly stronger fluorescence signals for both RITC and DiD compared with those from the GLL group. Quantitative analysis demonstrated that the GLCL group exhibited significantly higher RITC fluorescence intensity (P < 0.05; Figure c) and a trend toward increased DiD intensity (P = 0.08; Figure d). Furthermore, in the subtracted images (RITC–DiD), GLCL-treated tumors displayed higher and more homogeneous signals than GLL-treated ones, indicating deeper and more uniform intratumoral penetration of gemcitabine (Figure b). Finally, fluorescence heterogeneity analysis based on RITC intensity revealed that the GLCL group exhibited a more uniform signal distribution with significantly lower coefficients of variation (CV), whereas the GLL group showed pronounced spatial variability with higher CV values, indicating less homogeneous gemcitabine penetration (P < 0.05; Figure e).

These findings indicate that collagenase-mediated remodeling of the dense ECM facilitates the diffusion and convection of nanoparticles throughout the tumor interstitium, consistent with the enhanced accumulation observed in in vivo imaging. Notably, while both the liposomal carriers and their fluorescent tracers (DiD) penetrated more deeply following enzymatic stromal degradation, the encapsulated cargo (RITC) exhibited an even more homogeneous and extensive intratumoral distribution. This provides direct microscopic evidence that GLCL not only enhance nanoparticle transport but also promote deeper and more uniform delivery of the therapeutic payload, thereby overcoming the physical diffusion barrier characteristic of PDAC.

sec.title: Spatially Resolved Molecular Quantification of dFdU Following GLCL-Mediated Gemcitabine Delivery
sec.p: To obtain molecular evidence of enhanced gemcitabine delivery, DESI-MSI was employed to visualize and quantify the major inactive metabolite of gemcitabine, dFdU, within tumor sections. , Tumors were collected from KPCY 7160c5-bearing mice at 12 and 24 h after intravenous injection of normal saline (NS), free gemcitabine (FG), GLL, or GLCL, all at equivalent gemcitabine doses.

As shown in Figure a, tumor dFdU levels at 12 and 24 hours postinjection were assessed by DESI-MSI, with the GLCL-treated group exhibiting significantly higher signal intensities than the FG and GLL groups at both time points. At 12 h, the GLCL group showed a dFdU concentration of 6.44 ± 0.73 μM, which was notably higher than those in the NS (0 μM; P < 0.0001), FG (2.27 ± 0.41 μM; P < 0.001), and GLL (4.54 ± 1.36 μM) groups (Figure b, d). This enhanced dFdU accumulation was characterized by a more widespread spatial distribution throughout the tumor tissue. This trend persisted and became more pronounced at 24 h, with the GLCL group reaching a concentration of 9.4 ± 0.54 μM, remaining significantly higher than the levels in the NS (0 μM; P < 0.0001), FG (4.79 ± 1.15 μM; P < 0.01), and GLL (6.17 ± 1.44 μM; P < 0.05) groups (Figure c, d). Quantitative analysis revealed that the GLCL group had the highest normalized mean dFdU intensity per pixel, indicating its superior gemcitabine delivery efficiency. By contrast, the FG and GLL groups showed lower dFdU accumulation relative to the GLCL group, while the NS control group exhibited negligible signal, confirming the metabolite’s specificity to gemcitabine administration.

caption.p: Quantitative DESI-MSI analysis of the gemcitabine metabolite dFdU in tumor tissues of KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice (n = 3). (a) Optical images and corresponding DESI-MSI maps showing the intratumoral spatial distribution of dFdU in tumor tissues collected from NS, FG, GLL, and GLCL-treated mice at 12 and 24 h after intravenous injection using DESI-MSI. All scale bars indicate a length of 1 mm. (b, c) Quantitative analysis of intratumoral dFdU concentrations at 12 and 24 h, respectively. (d) Summary comparison of intratumoral dFdU concentrations at 12 and 24 h across all groups. Data were statistically analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test (n = 3, mean ± SD). *: P < 0.05, **: P < 0.01, ***: P < 0.001, ****: P < 0.0001.

sec.p: These quantitative and spatially resolved data confirm that GLCL markedly enhances the intratumoral delivery and metabolic retention of gemcitabine compared with both free and liposomal formulations lacking collagenase. Importantly, this represents the first demonstration of nanocarrier-mediated gemcitabine penetration in PDAC at the molecular level, directly visualized by DESI-MSI after intravenous administration. By bridging fluorescence-based imaging and molecular quantification, DESI-MSI establishes a mechanistic link between collagenase-driven stromal remodeling and enhanced drug distribution within desmoplastic pancreatic tumors.

Compared to previous in vivo imaging system (IVIS)-based biodistribution or other tumor penetration studies, which visualize fluorescently labeled nanocarriers or drugs indirectly, DESI-MSI provides a more precise and spatially resolved assessment of the actual accumulation of drug metabolites. −
Notably, dFdU was selected as the target analyte instead of gemcitabine itself because gemcitabine is rapidly deaminated in vivo by cytidine deaminase and has a short plasma half-life following intravenous infusion, making direct postmortem detection unreliable. −
By comparison, dFdU exhibits a longer half-life and more stable retention in tissues. −
Therefore, quantifying dFdU in postmortem tumor sections provides a more reliable and representative indicator of gemcitabine distribution and metabolism in vivo. To our knowledge, dFdU imaging in tumors has only been reported once previously, in a study where free gemcitabine was administered intraperitoneally and analyzed at 2 h postinjection. In contrast, the present work represents the first demonstration of dFdU quantification within tumor tissues following intravenous administration of a liposomal gemcitabine formulation, specifically collagenase-functionalized GLCL, with extended time points up to 24 h. This distinction highlights the strength of our approach and underscores its value in directly assessing not only nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery but also the prolonged metabolic fate of gemcitabine in vivo.

sec.title: Radiolabeling Efficiency and In Vivo PET Evaluation of 64Cu-GLCL in KPCY 7160c5 Tumor-Bearing Mice
sec.p: Following fluorescence- and mass-spectrometry-based analyses, in vivo positron emission tomography (PET) was performed to further evaluate the quantitative pharmacokinetics and tumor-targeting behavior of GLCL in vivo. High radiolabeling efficiency of 64Cu-GLCL was first confirmed, reaching 98.6% immediately after synthesis. Radiochemical stability remained high, with 99.8% and 100% of the radioactivity retained at 2 and 24 h, respectively (Figure S6a).

PET imaging of 64Cu-GLCL in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice revealed sustained blood circulation and progressive tumor accumulation over 24 h (Figure b). The circulation half-life of 64Cu-GLCL was calculated to be 11.80 h, and tumor uptake gradually increased over 24 h, reaching 5.80 ± 1.07%ID/g (Figure S6b, c). At 24 h postinjection, the uptake in nontarget organs, heart, liver, spleen, and muscle, was 3.27 ± 0.60, 28.53 ± 2.80, 4.94 ± 0.39, and 1.42 ± 0.11%ID/g, respectively (Figure S6d–g). The tumor-to-organ ratios for heart, liver, spleen, and muscle showed an increasing trend over time, reaching 1.80 ± 0.35, 1.17 ± 0.12, 0.20 ± 0.03, and 4.08 ± 0.63, respectively, at 24 h postinjection (Figure c–f). These data demonstrate that 64Cu-GLCL maintains high radiochemical stability, prolonged systemic circulation, and efficient tumor accumulation. Because PET enables absolute quantification of radiotracer distribution and is already established in clinical oncology imaging, these results provide translational confirmation that GLCL’s pharmacokinetic and targeting properties can be noninvasively monitored using a clinically relevant modality.

caption.p: In vivo PET imaging of 64Cu-labeled GLCL for quantitative biodistribution analysis in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice. (a) Schematic illustration of the radiolabeling strategy and preparation of 64Cu-GLCL. (b) Representative whole-body PET images of KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice acquired at 0, 2, 12, and 24 h after intravenous administration of 64Cu-GLCL (n = 3). Tumor regions are indicated by white circles. (c–f) Time-dependent tumor-to-organ uptake ratios of 64Cu-GLCL for the heart (c), liver (d), spleen (e), and muscle (f), calculated from PET-derived %ID/g values (n = 3, mean ± SD).

sec.p: Collectively, the PET findings offer independent, quantitative validation of the GLCL platform’s favorable biodistribution and long-circulating profile, highlighting its potential as a clinically translatable theranostic nanocarrier that combines diagnostic traceability with effective drug delivery. −

sec.title: Therapeutic Efficacy, Safety, and Translational Considerations of GLCL
sec.p: The therapeutic potential of GLCL was evaluated in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice following the imaging studies. Tumor growth and body weight were monitored throughout the treatment period (Figure b, c). As a result, the tumor size in the GLCL-treated group was significantly smaller than that in the NS (P < 0.0001), FG (P < 0.01), and GLL (P < 0.001) groups. Additionally, the tumor growth inhibition rates for GLCL, GLL, and FG were 69.75%, 10.89%, and 41.76%, respectively (Figure d, e). These results demonstrate the superior antitumor efficacy of GLCL compared to the other groups. Histological analysis provided additional insight into treatment outcomes. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining revealed more extensive tumor necrosis in GLCL-treated mice compared with other groups, while Masson’s trichrome (MT) staining showed markedly reduced blue staining corresponding to collagen fibers in GLCL-treated tumors (Figure f). Quantitative image analysis of MT-stained tumor sections demonstrated that the collagen-positive area (% of tissue area) was significantly lower in the GLCL group than in the NS group (P < 0.0001; Figure S7a, b) and was also significantly reduced compared with the FG and GLL groups (P < 0.001; Figure S7a, b).

caption.p: Comparative therapeutic effects in KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice treated with NS, FG, GLL, or GLCL. (a) Schematic illustration of the treatment procedure. Mice (n = 5 per group) received intravenous injections of NS, FG, GLL, or GLCL every other day for 20 days. (b) Tumor size and (c) body weight of mice measured during the treatment period (mean ± SD). Data were analyzed by one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. **: P < 0.01, ***: P < 0.001, ****: P < 0.0001. (d) In vivo tumor growth inhibition by FG, GLL, and GLCL. (e) Representative tumor images from each group on the final day. (f) Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E, upper row) and Masson’s trichrome (MT, lower row) staining of tumor sections from each group. Scale bar: 100 μm.

sec.p:
Notably, despite PEGylation being generally known to enhance nanoparticle circulation time and tumor accumulation, GLL exhibited lower antitumor efficacy compared to FG. This unexpected outcome can be explained by the accelerated blood clearance (ABC) phenomenon. Upon repeated intravenous administration of maleimide-containing liposomes, the immune system may recognize these nanoparticles, leading to their rapid clearance during subsequent administrations, ultimately reducing therapeutic effectiveness. −
In this study, GLL was designed to match GLCL in molar ratios and particle size, with the sole difference being the absence of collagenase conjugation. This design ensured experimental consistency but also led to the exposure of unreacted maleimide moieties on the surface of GLL. Consequently, unreacted maleimide moieties remained exposed on the GLL surface, potentially forming nonspecific covalent bonds with free thiol residues of abundant plasma proteins such as albumin and immunoglobulins. −
This nonspecific interaction likely results in the formation of a protein corona on the liposomal surface, facilitating recognition by the immune system, promoting rapid phagocytosis, and accelerating clearance via the reticuloendothelial system (RES). , Thus, repeated administrations may exacerbate the ABC effect, contributing significantly to the diminished therapeutic efficacy observed for GLL. This interpretation aligns with previous studies indicating that maleimide groups on PEGylated liposome surfaces can induce nonspecific protein binding and subsequent immune activation. ,,

The reduced efficacy of GLL can be mechanistically attributed to maleimide-associated immune recognition and ABC-mediated clearance under the current experimental settings. However, additional immunological considerations may emerge during the clinical translation of stromal-modulating nanotherapeutic platforms.

One such translational immunological consideration is the bacterial origin of collagenolytic enzymes. It is noteworthy that collagenolytic enzymes derived from Clostridium histolyticum have already achieved clinical translation, as exemplified by FDA-approved collagenase Clostridium histolyticum formulations (e.g., Xiaflex, Qwo), thereby supporting the translational feasibility of bacterial collagenases as a drug class. −
However, despite this established clinical precedent, immunogenicity-associated adverse events, including antidrug antibody formation, hypersensitivity reactions, and systemic inflammatory responses, have been reported for bacterial enzyme-based therapeutics in certain clinical contexts. , These observations indicate that bacterial origin remains a nontrivial immunological liability, particularly under repeated or chronic dosing regimens, and therefore warrants careful consideration in the translational engineering of collagenase-functionalized nanotherapeutics. ,

To mitigate these translational risks, several engineering strategies can be envisioned for future clinical development. First, substitution with recombinant human collagenases or human matrix metalloproteinases (e.g., MMP-1) may further minimize immunogenicity and improve clinical compatibility. −
Second, epitope-selective surface shielding of collagenase via site-specific PEGylation or zwitterionic polymer conjugation could sterically mask dominant immunogenic epitopes and reduce immune recognition while preserving enzymatic activity. −
Third, incorporation of tumor-responsive cleavable linkers in combination with steric masking moieties to enable tumor-localized unmasking could spatially confine collagenolytic activity, thereby minimizing systemic exposure and off-target immunogenic risks while maximizing intratumoral stromal modulation. −
Collectively, these considerations highlight critical translational design parameters for advancing GLCL toward clinically applicable stromal-modulating nanotherapeutic platforms.

Given the superior therapeutic efficacy of GLCL, we compared its formulation characteristics with those of previously reported gemcitabine-based nanoparticle systems, as summarized in Table , focusing on parameters including particle size, loading efficiency (LE), loading capacity (LC), route of administration, and injection dose. Yu et al. formulated gemcitabine-loaded nanoparticles using human serum albumin (Gem-HSA-NPs), which exhibited a particle size of 150 ± 27 nm, an LE of 82.99% ± 3.5%, and an LC of 10.42% ± 3.5%. Gemcitabine was administered at 50 mg/kg. Inkoom et al. converted gemcitabine into a stable prodrug form, 4NSG, and developed solid lipid nanoparticles (4NSG-SLN) with a particle size of 82 ± 6.7 nm. This formulation achieved a high LE of 98.7 ± 4.5%, although the LC was not reported, with gemcitabine administered at 30 mg/kg. Lin et al. reported dendrimer-gold hybrid nanoparticles (Gem-Au DENPs) coloaded with gemcitabine and a miR-21 inhibitor (miR-21i), with particle sizes ranging from 154 to 276 nm. Although the LE was not specified, the LC was estimated to be approximately 30 gemcitabine molecules per dendrimer. The gemcitabine dose in this study was 10 mg/kg. Karaca et al. designed micelle-form nanoparticles (mPEG-b-PCC-g-GEM-g-DC), in which gemcitabine was chemically conjugated to the polymer backbone and vismodegib (GDC-0449) was encapsulated. These nanoparticles had a particle size of 36 nm and an LC of 14%, though the LE was not reported. Gemcitabine was administered at 40 mg/kg. Meng et al. developed a dual-drug delivery system by coloading gemcitabine and paclitaxel into lipid bilayer-coated mesoporous silica nanoparticles (LB-MSNPs), with a particle size of 65 nm. The LC was reported as 40%, while the LE was not specified. The gemcitabine dose used in this study was 100 mg/kg. In comparison, the GLCL nanoparticles developed in this study demonstrated a uniform particle size of 50.77 ± 16.76 nm, along with an acceptable drug loading efficiency of 15.3%. Notably, despite the substantially lower gemcitabine dose of 6.75 mg/kg, approximately 1.5- to 15-fold lower than those used in previous studies, GLCL achieved superior tumor growth inhibition. These findings underscore the pivotal role of collagenase-mediated ECM remodeling in enhancing intratumoral drug delivery and therapeutic efficacy. These cross-study comparisons indicate that GLCL achieves superior antitumor efficacy despite a comparatively modest drug loading efficiency, a finding that deviates from the commonly observed correlation between payload capacity and therapeutic efficacy and thus warrants further discussion regarding its formulation rationale, translational implications, and potential optimization space. Importantly, the relatively modest drug loading efficiency of GLCL should be interpreted within the context of its rational formulation design strategy, which prioritizes intratumoral delivery efficiency enabled by stromal remodeling rather than payload maximization. In this framework, effective collagenase-mediated ECM modulation requires that a sufficient number of enzyme-functionalized nanoparticles reach and penetrate tumor tissues. However, even sterically stabilized liposomes are preferentially sequestered by the mononuclear phagocyte system (MPS), particularly in the liver and spleen, which substantially limits the fraction of injected nanoparticles capable of accessing tumors. , Accordingly, under a fixed lipid dose, increasing particle size may increase the internal aqueous volume and apparent drug loading capacity, but it simultaneously reduces the absolute number of circulating particles that can reach tumor tissues. In contrast, smaller nanoparticles provide a higher particle number density, thereby increasing the probability of tumor access and homogeneous intratumoral distribution. −
Therefore, GLCL was formulated with a relatively small particle size (∼50 nm) to maximize tumor-reachable particle numbers, which inherently constrains the achievable gemcitabine loading capacity. Moreover, deep tumor penetration and homogeneous intratumoral drug distribution require not only effective tumor accumulation but also high colloidal stability during systemic circulation. As demonstrated in Figure a, GLCL prepared with 11 mM gemcitabine and 70 μM collagenase exhibited the lowest PDI and the highest colloidal stability, representing an optimized balance between enzyme functionality and nanoparticle stability. This stability-prioritized formulation design further constrains the maximum attainable drug loading efficiency.

sec.p: From a translational and manufacturing perspective, this design paradigm implies that drug loading efficiency is an important determinant of drug-to-lipid mass ratio, infusion volume, excipient exposure, and production cost. , However, in the GLCL system, our data demonstrate that collagenase-mediated ECM remodeling markedly enhances intratumoral drug bioavailability, thereby substantially reducing the systemic gemcitabine dose required to achieve therapeutic efficacy. Consequently, under the present dosing paradigm, the relatively modest loading efficiency of GLCL is not expected to impose a clinically unfavorable lipid burden or manufacturing disadvantage. Nevertheless, the GLCL formulation retains substantial room for further optimization toward future translational development. Potential optimization strategies include (i) pH-gradient-based remote loading, (ii) modulation of intraliposomal buffer composition and pH, (iii) tuning of lipid composition and ratios (e.g., DSPC/Chol/PEG), and (iv) development of lipidized gemcitabine prodrugs. These strategies represent realistic and systematic optimization pathways to progressively enhance drug loading while preserving the ECM-remodeling delivery framework and tumor accessibility of GLCL.

In addition to therapeutic efficacy, the in vivo toxicity of the nanoparticle formulations was evaluated to assess their biocompatibility and systemic safety. Accordingly, major organs (lungs, heart, kidneys, liver, and spleen) were subjected to histological analysis using H&E staining after treatment. The results revealed no observable tissue damage, suggesting excellent biocompatibility of the nanoparticles (Figure S8). To further evaluate systemic safety, blood biochemical analysis was conducted during therapeutic experiments to assess hepatotoxicity (ALT, AST) and nephrotoxicity (CREA, BUN), providing insight into the in vivo toxicity associated with repeated intravenous administration of the nanoparticles. The results demonstrated that FG, GLL, and GLCL showed no significant differences from the NS group, indicating no observable hepatic or renal toxicity (Figure S9).

Together, these results demonstrate that GLCL achieves a potent antitumor effect through collagenase-mediated ECM remodeling, enhanced gemcitabine penetration, and efficient tumor growth suppression without systemic toxicity. When integrated with the preceding in vivo fluorescence, DESI-MSI, and PET analyses, these findings establish a comprehensive and quantitative validation pipeline, spanning molecular imaging to therapeutic efficacy, that highlights the translational potential of GLCL chemotherapy for stroma-rich pancreatic cancer.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In summary, we developed GLCL that enzymatically remodels the collagen-rich fibrotic ECM barrier characteristic of PDAC. By integrating enzymatic matrix degradation with efficient drug delivery, GLCL overcame the diffusion limitations imposed by fibrotic ECM and enabled deeper and more homogeneous intratumoral penetration of gemcitabine.

A series of complementary analyses, including in vivo fluorescence imaging, ex vivo confocal microscopy, quantitative DESI-MSI, and PET imaging, collectively provided multiscale and molecular-level evidence that GLCL enhances both tumor accumulation and metabolic retention of the drug. Importantly, DESI-MSI established the first direct molecular validation of nanocarrier-mediated drug penetration in PDAC, also establishing a new framework to evaluate the metabolic fate of chemotherapeutics in solid tumors, while PET imaging confirmed the pharmacokinetic and tumor-targeting behavior in a quantitative and clinically translatable manner.

Therapeutic studies further demonstrated that GLCL achieved superior tumor growth inhibition and collagen depletion without systemic toxicity. Together, these findings define GLCL as a functionally active and clinically relevant nanoplatform capable of overcoming the collagen-dominant stromal ECM diffusion barrier and improving the efficacy of chemotherapeutics in stroma-rich malignancies.

sec.title: Methods
Materials
sec.p: 1,2-Distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC; 18:0 PC), 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[amino­(polyethylene glycol)-2000] (DSPE-PEG2k-Amine), and 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (methoxy­(polyethylene glycol)-2000) (DSPE-mPEG2k) were purchased from Avanti Polar Lipids, Inc. (Alabama, USA). 1,2-Distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[maleimide­(polyethylene glycol)-2000] (DSPE-PEG2k-Mal) was acquired from Creative PEGWorks (North Carolina, USA). Collagenase type I (powder), EnzChek Gelatinase/Collagenase Assay Kit, 1,1′-dioctadecyl-3,3,3′,3′-Tetramethylindodicarbocyanine Perchlorate (DiD’ oil; DiIC18(5) oil), 1,1′-dioctadecyl-3,3,3′,3′-Tetramethylindotricarbocyanine Iodide (DiR’; DiIC18(7)), and 0.4% Trypan Blue Solution were obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific Korea, Inc. (Seoul, Korea). Gemcitabine hydrochloride ≥ 98% (HPLC, GEM), fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC), Rhodamine B-isothiocyanate (RITC), Nile red, cholesterol, N,N-diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA; DIEA), Ninhydrin ACS reagent, Spectra-Por Float-A-Lyzer G2 Dialysis Device (MWCO: 100 kDa), Amicon Ultra Centrifugal Filter Unit (MWCO: 100 kDa), acetonitrile, and dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, Ltd. (Missouri, USA). Ethanol, methanol, chloroform, and DMSO were acquired from Deajung Chemicals & Metals Co., Ltd. (Siheung, Korea). ViaFluor 488 Live Cell Microtubule Staining Kit was purchased from Biotium (Fremont, California). 2-(p-Isothiocyanatobenzyl)-1,4,7-triazacyclononane-N,N′,N″-triacetic acid trihydrochloride ((p-SCN-Bn)-NOTA) was obtained from FUTURECHEM (Seoul, Korea). Instant thin-layer chromatography medium with silica gel (iTLC-SG) was acquired from Agilent Technologies, Inc. (Santa Clara, CA, USA). BALB/c nude female mice (4–8 weeks) were procured from Orient Bio 134 (Seongnam, Korea).

sec.title: Instruments
sec.p: NanoDrop 2000/2000c Spectrophotometer (NanoDrop 2000, Thermo Fisher Scientific Korea, Inc., Seoul, Korea) was used to quantify gemcitabine and collagenase type I. The hydrodynamic sizes of GLCL and GLL were measured using dynamic light scattering (DLS; Zetasizer Nano-ZS ZEN 1020, Malvern Panalytical Ltd., Grovewood Road, UK). TEM images of nanoparticles were obtained using an energy-filtering transmission electron microscope (EF-TEM, LIBRA 120, Carl Zeiss Co., Ltd., Oberkochen, Germany). The collagenase purification process was carried out using a high-speed centrifuge (Centrifuge, 1248, GYROGEN Co., Ltd., Daejeon, Korea). A microplate reader (Synergy H1 hybrid multimode reader, BioTek Instruments, Vermont, USA) was employed to perform the collagenase kinetic assay and the ninhydrin assay. A fluorescence spectrometer (FS-2, Scinco Co., Ltd., Seoul, Korea) was used for the FRET assay to verify collagenase type I attachment. A confocal microscope (Nikon A1R+ACC, Nikon Co., Tokyo, Japan) was utilized to evaluate the cellular uptake of nanoparticles (in vitro) and to assess their penetration into tumor tissue based on the types of particles administered to mice (in vivo). Desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging (DESI-MSI) was performed using a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc., MA, USA). Fluorescence images of mice, both in vivo and ex vivo, were acquired using the IVIS Spectrum imaging system (IVIS Spectrum, PerkinElmer, Inc., Massachusetts, USA). The in vivo biodistribution of 64Cu-GLCL in tumor-bearing mice was examined using a SimPET/MRI (M7, Bringtonix Imaging, Inc., Seoul, Korea), and the images were analyzed using the MIM-64-bit program (MIM software, Inc., Ohio, USA).

sec.title: Preparation and Characterization of GLCL
sec.p: GLCL were prepared using the following method: The lipids, DSPC, DSPE-PEG-Maleimide (2k), DSPE-mPEG (2k), and cholesterol, were dissolved at a weight ratio of 6:6:1:0.5 in a 2:1 (v/v) chloroform:methanol solvent mixture. Subsequently, the organic solvents were gently evaporated using nitrogen gas in a chemical hood, and any residual solvents were further removed by keeping the mixture in a vacuum evaporator overnight. Afterward, an 11 mM gemcitabine solution in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was added to the dried lipid film and subjected to tip sonication for 12 min. The resulting liposomes were filtered through a 0.2 μm syringe filter to remove large aggregates and obtain a uniform particle size distribution. Finally, 70 μM collagenase type I was added to the syringe-filtered liposomes and gently mixed at pH 7.4 and 37 °C for 3 h to facilitate the maleimide-amine reaction between collagenase and DSPE-PEG-Maleimide (2k) in the GLCL. The conjugated liposomes were then processed through a 100 K Amicon tube to remove free gemcitabine and collagenase. The washing was repeated until free gemcitabine and collagenase could no longer be detected in the filtrate. A schematic representation of the overall GLCL synthesis is presented in Figure a.

The gemcitabine loading efficiency (LE) and loading capacity (LC) were calculated using the following equations: LE=(mgem,encapsulatedmgem,initial)×100%
LC=(mgem,encapsulatedmlipid,total)×100% where m gem,encapsulated is the amount of gemcitabine encapsulated in GLCL, m gem,initial is the total amount of gemcitabine added initially, and m lipid,total is the total lipid weight used.

Similarly, the conjugation efficiency (CE) of collagenase type I on the liposomal surface was calculated using the following equation: CE=(mcoll,total−mcoll,freemcoll,total)×100% where m coll,total is the total amount of collegenase added and m coll,free is the amount of free (unbound) collagenase in the filtrate.

For the control group, GLL, the step involving the reaction with collagenase was omitted; nonetheless, similar to GLCL, GLL underwent the same filtration process using a 100 K Amicon tube to eliminate free gemcitabine. For the tumor penetration and in vivo imaging tests, GLCL and GLL were synthesized and purified following the same method described above, by codissolving the distinct fluorescent dyes and the lipid mixture during the initial preparation step. For the tumor penetration test, DiD (23.76 μM; stock: 5 mg/mL in EtOH) and RITC (642.05 μM; stock: 5 mg/100 μL in DMSO) were prepared at a 1:1 volume ratio (v/v). For in vivo imaging, DiR (19.7 μM; stock: 2 mg/mL in EtOH) was used.

sec.title: Particle Size and Morphology Analysis of GLCL and GLL
sec.p: To determine the hydrodynamic sizes of the synthesized GLCL and GLL, DLS was employed. In addition, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using an energy-filtering transmission electron microscope (EF-TEM) for detailed evaluation of particle size and morphology. All samples were deposited onto glow-discharged grids and then negatively stained with 2% uranyl acetate solution.

sec.title: Particle Size Stability of GLCL and GLL
sec.p: The size stability of GLCL and GLL was evaluated by monitoring changes in particle size and PDI over 7 days. Samples were diluted in PBS at a 1:9 ratio and analyzed by DLS at both room temperature and 37 °C. Measurements were performed on days 0, 3, 5, and 7, and all values were normalized to those obtained on day 0 (the day of synthesis).

sec.title: Verification of Collagenase Surface Conjugation to GLCL via FRET Assay
sec.p: FRET assay was conducted using FITC (donor) and Nile red (acceptor) to confirm the surface conjugation of collagenase to GLCL. For the experimental group, 0.1 mM Nile red was incorporated into the lipid bilayer of GLCL, followed by conjugation with 70 μM collagenase under the same maleimide–amine coupling conditions described in the synthesis section (37 °C, pH 7.4, 3 h). The samples were then purified using a 100 K Amicon tube. Subsequently, they were incubated with 85.6 μM FITC at 37 °C and pH 7.4 overnight to allow FITC to bind to collagenase. Free FITC was removed by dialysis using a 100 K dialysis tube overnight. As control groups, two formulations were prepared: one with GLCL conjugated with only FITC-labeled collagenase, and another with GLCL loaded with only Nile red, which the conjugated collagenase was not labeled with FITC. Both formulations were synthesized and purified using the same procedure as the experimental group. To ensure consistency, all three groups were treated with equal concentrations of fluorescent dyes, FITC (85.6 μM) and Nile red (0.1 mM), which were mixed in a 1:1 volume ratio (v/v). All samples were excited at approximately λex = 490 nm, the excitation wavelength of FITC, and the emission spectra were recorded from 500 to 750 nm using photoluminescence spectroscopy (PL). The FRET efficiency was calculated using the following equation: 1 E=1−IDAID where I DA represents the intensity of the donor in the presence of the acceptor, and I D represents the intensity of the donor in the absence of the acceptor. The distance (R) between FITC (donor) and Nile red (acceptor) was calculated using the following equation: 2 R=R0[(1/E)−1]1/6 In this equation, E represents the FRET efficiency, and R 0 = 58.83 Å, a value determined using the FRET calculator.

sec.title: Quantitative Analysis of Amino Group Substitution in Collagenase-Conjugated GLCL by Ninhydrin Assay
sec.p: To evaluate the degree of collagenase conjugation on the GLCL surface, a ninhydrin assay was performed by comparing the amino group content between free collagenase and GLCL. A standard curve was generated through serial dilution, with both samples prepared at identical concentrations ranging from 0 to 25 μM. Ninhydrin solution was formulated by dissolving 0.2 g of ninhydrin in 10 mL of ethanol to achieve a final concentration of 2%. The serially diluted samples were mixed with the ninhydrin solution at a 1:2 ratio and then incubated at 95 °C for 15 min. After the reaction, all samples were cooled to room temperature. Absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader and used to construct a linear regression curve by plotting absorbance (y) against sample concentration (x). The degree of amine group substitution was quantified by comparing the slopes of the linear regression lines for free collagenase and GLCL. Collagenase type I, an enzyme originally isolated from the bacterium Clostridium histolyticum, was assumed to possess 100% of its amine groups in free form, and its slope was used as the reference. The percentage of amino group substitution was calculated using the following formula: ΔStotal=SfreecollagenasetypeIΔS=SfreecollagenasetypeI−SGLCL%⁡substitution=(ΔSΔStotal)×100%

sec.title: Assessment of Enzymatic Activity and Stability of Surface-Conjugated Collagenase on GLCL via DQ Gelatin-Based Fluorescence Assay
sec.p: The enzymatic activity of collagenase immobilized on the GLCL surface was assessed using the EnzChek Gelatinase/Collagenase Assay Kit, which employs fluorescein-conjugated gelatin (DQ gelatin) that emits fluorescence upon proteolytic cleavage, enabling kinetic evaluation of collagenase activity (Figure S2a). For the kinetic assay, 100 μL of each sample was mixed with 80 μL of 1× reaction buffer and 20 μL of DQ gelatin to obtain a final reaction volume of 200 μL. Four groups were analyzed in parallel: (i) the kit-provided collagenase standard (collagenase type IV), (ii) free collagenase type I, (iii) GLCL, and (iv) GLL. After incubation under standardized conditions, fluorescence intensity was measured at an emission wavelength of 515 nm and monitored over time, with 800 min selected as a fixed end point for comparative analysis across all samples.

For calibration, the kit-provided collagenase type IV standard was prepared at a maximum activity of 0.5 U and serially diluted to generate a broad range of enzyme activity units, and fluorescence intensities measured at a fixed reaction time point (800 min) were used to construct a multipoint calibration curve. Enzymatic activity was quantified by fitting the end point fluorescence values of the calibration standards to a nonlinear regression model, and the activities of free collagenase type I and GLCL were determined by applying their end point fluorescence intensities, measured at 800 min, to the resulting calibration function. Enzymatic activities were expressed in the manufacturer-defined activity unit system referenced to the collagenase type IV standard. Because the assay kit defines enzymatic activity units based on a collagenase type IV standard, the activities of free collagenase type I and GLCL were reported as collagenase type IV–equivalent units, defined as the activity of the kit-provided collagenase type IV that yields the same fluorescence response under identical assay conditions.

To assess enzymatic stability, collagenase activity of GLCL was evaluated using the same DQ gelatin-based fluorescence assay principle and reaction composition as described for the kinetic assay, but quantified using a simplified single-time-point measurement. GLCL samples derived from the same original batch were stored at room temperature or 37 °C and sequentially sampled at days 0, 1, 3, 5, and 7. Fluorescence intensity was measured after a fixed reaction time (10 min), and the retained enzymatic activity was expressed as a percentage relative to the corresponding activity measured at day 0.

sec.title: Cell Lines and Culture Conditions
sec.p: KPCY 7160c5 and Panc-1 cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator. The medium was supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1% antibiotics, 4500 mg/L d-glucose, l-glutamine, 110 mg/L sodium pyruvate, and sodium bicarbonate.

sec.title: Comparative Cytotoxicity and Cellular Uptake Analysis of GLCL and GLL
sec.p: KPCY 7160c5 and Panc-1 cells were seeded into 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 104 cells per well and incubated for 24 h to allow cell attachment. For free gemcitabine, the cells were treated with concentrations ranging from 0 to 2 mg/mL and incubated for 48 h. To determine the IC50 value, the concentration data were log-transformed and plotted to generate dose–response curves. In contrast, GLL and GLCL were applied at equivalent gemcitabine concentrations ranging from 0 to 37.5 μg/mL for the same duration. After the treatment period, 100 μL of MTT solution (0.5 mg/mL thiazolyl blue tetrazolium bromide) was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 6 h. Following incubation, 100 μL of DMSO was added to each well to dissolve the resulting formazan deposits. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader to assess cell viability. The absorbance values obtained from the GLL and GLCL samples were statistically analyzed using a two-sided Student’s t-test.

Based on the cytotoxicity results obtained from the MTT assay, the time-dependent cellular uptake of GLCL and GLL was comparatively evaluated in KPCY 7160 cells, the representative cell line chosen for subsequent therapeutic experiments. KPCY 7160c5 cells were seeded at a density of 1.5 × 104 cells per confocal dish and incubated for 24 h to allow cell attachment. Subsequently, equal amounts (DiD 23.76 μM) of the synthesized DiD-labeled GLCL and DiD-labeled GLL were applied and incubated for 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h, respectively. After each incubation period, Hoechst 33342 and ViaFluor 488 were added to stain the nuclei and cytoskeleton, respectively, and the samples were incubated for 40 min. After each sample and fluorescent dye treatment step, cells were washed three times with Dulbecco’s Phosphate-Buffered Saline (DPBS). Following completion of all treatments, cells were finally fixed with 4% PFA for approximately 30 min. Cellular uptake was subsequently analyzed using confocal microscopy.

sec.title: Establishment of Tumor-Bearing Mouse Models
sec.p: Six-week-old BALB/c nude female mice were subcutaneously injected in the right thigh with 1 × 106 KPCY 7160c5 cells. KPCY 7160c5 models were used for fluorescence-based penetration analysis, in vivo IVIS and PET imaging, and therapeutic studies. All procedures were conducted under 2% isoflurane anesthesia.

All animal procedures were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Seoul National University Hospital (approval no. SNU-260112–5) and were conducted in accordance with the relevant institutional guidelines and regulations.

sec.title: IVIS Fluorescence Imaging for Biodistribution Analysis
sec.p: DiR-labeled GLCL and GLL were intravenously injected into BALB/c nude female mice (n = 5) modeled with KPCY 7160c5 cell lines for fluorescence imaging. In vivo fluorescence imaging was performed at 0, 2, 6, 12, and 24 h postinjection, followed by sacrifice of the mice to obtain ex vivo imaging of the tumor, liver, lung, spleen, heart, and kidney.

Prior to injection, the fluorescence intensities of DiR-labeled GLCL and GLL were measured to account for formulation-dependent differences (Figure S4a). To minimize potential imaging bias arising from differences in initial fluorescence intensity, the minimum and maximum display scales for in vivo fluorescence images were adjusted proportionally for each formulation. All ex vivo fluorescence images were quantified using the Living Image 64-bit software. The comparison of tumor-to-organ ratios was analyzed statistically using a two-sided Student’s t-test.

sec.title: Tumor Penetration Assessment of GLCL via Dual Fluorescent Tracking
sec.p: To further validate the intratumoral penetration of GLCL observed in the previous IVIS imaging experiment, an independent in vivo validation experiment using KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice was employed. GLCL, GLL, and NS were intravenously administered to the mice. All injected liposomal formulations were labeled with the fluorescent dyes DiD and RITC to visually assess nanoparticle penetration into tumor tissues. DiD was incorporated into the lipid bilayer to trace the distribution of the nanoparticles (GLL or GLCL), and RITC was coloaded with gemcitabine in the aqueous core to monitor drug localization. At 12 h postinjection, all tumors were harvested. Tumor tissues were then embedded in OCT compound, and cryosections were prepared from the central region of each tumor at a thickness of 4 μm to ensure consistent intratumoral sampling. The tissue sections were mounted on glass slides and fixed in methanol for 30 min. Fluorescence signals within the tumors were subsequently analyzed and compared using confocal microscopy.

Quantitative analysis of intratumoral fluorescence heterogeneity was performed on tumor sections designated as GLCL and GLL. Pixel-level red-channel intensities were extracted from grayscale-converted images, and statistical indices including mean, standard deviation, and coefficient of variation (CV) were computed using Python 3.11. The red channel from RITC images and the blue channel from DiD images were extracted, converted to float arrays, and min–max normalized (0–1). Pixel-wise subtraction was performed as Isub(x,y)=IRITC(x,y)−IDiD(x,y) with negative values clipped to zero. Subtraction images were rescaled to 8-bit (0–255) and visualized as heatmaps with a common intensity scale bar.

sec.title: DESI-MSI-Based Spatial and Quantitative Analysis of dFdU in Tumor Tissues
sec.p: To assess intratumoral gemcitabine delivery and distribution, DESI-MSI was performed to quantify its major metabolite, dFdU, in tumor tissues following GLCL administration. KPCY 7160c5 tumor-bearing mice were intravenously injected with NS, free gemcitabine (FG), GLL, or GLCL, with each gemcitabine-containing group (FG, GLL, and GLCL) receiving an identical dose of 6.75 mg/kg. Tumors were collected at 12 and 24 h postinjection following euthanasia. After harvesting, tumors were stored at −80 °C, and cryosections with a thickness of 10 μm were prepared from the central region of each tumor using a cryomicrotome. The sections were mounted on glass slides and dried for approximately 10 min in a vacuum desiccator prior to imaging. DESI-MSI was performed using a Q-Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer operated in negative ion mode. Spectra were acquired over m/z 150–1000 at a resolution of 140,000. A 1:1 (v/v) mixture of acetonitrile and DMF was used as the spray solvent (5 μL/min). The electrospray voltage was 5 kV, and capillary/cone voltages were 44–60 V. The sprayer was positioned 2 mm above the sample surface and 5 mm away from the MS inlet, with a spray angle of 75°. Imaging was conducted at 100 μm spatial resolution and a scan speed of 150 μm/s. Data were processed using Datacube Explorer (FOM Institute AMOLF). For quantitative analysis of dFdU in tumor tissue by DESI-MSI, a calibration curve was constructed using dFdU standard solutions. The matrix-matched calibration curve was constructed by depositing three concentrations of dFdU standard solutions (1, 5, and 10 μM) onto gemcitabine-untreated tumor tissue sections (Figure S5). Each concentration was analyzed in triplicate, and all tissue sections were measured under the same DESI-MSI conditions. dFdU ion intensities were measured from tissue sections treated with dFdU standards at known concentrations. Normalization of the dFdU signal was performed to generate a calibration curve relating normalized dFdU ion intensity to dFdU concentration. Normalized dFdU ion intensity (I dFdU,norm) was calculated as the average dFdU ion intensity per dFdU-positive pixel normalized to the average total ion current (TIC) per total tissue pixels. Specifically, normalization was performed using the following formula: IdFdU,norm=IdFdU,total/Npixels,dFdU+TIC/Npixels,tissue where I dFdU,total is the total dFdU ion intensity, N pixels,dFdU+ is the number of dFdU-positive pixels, and N pixels,tissue is the number of tissue pixels.

The calibration curve was fitted by linear regression (y = 0.84x – 0.93, R 2 = 0.98). This regression equation was subsequently used to convert normalized dFdU ion intensities measured in tumor tissues into absolute dFdU concentrations.

sec.title: Radiolabeling of GLCL with 64Cu: Evaluation of Labeling Efficiency and Stability
sec.p: Radiolabeling of GLCL with 64Cu was initiated by reacting 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[amino­(polyethylene glycol)-2000] (DSPE-PEG2k-Amine) with the chelator (p-SCN-Bn)-NOTA at a molar ratio of 1:1.5. The reaction mixture was subsequently incubated at room temperature for 24 h in the presence of N,N-diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA) as a catalyst. The resulting product was then combined with the GLCL premixture dissolved in an organic solvent. Subsequent formulation steps were carried out according to previously described GLCL synthesis protocols. In the next step, the 64Cu­(II) solution (64CuCl2) was adjusted to pH 7.4 using 1 M sodium acetate, and then mixed with the NOTA-conjugated GLCL, followed by incubation at 37 °C for 1 h with constant stirring. After the reaction, the solution was purified by size-exclusion chromatography using a PD-10 column to remove unbound 64Cu. The overall radiolabeling and synthesis process is schematically illustrated in Figure a. To evaluate radiolabeling efficiency and stability, 2 μL of 64Cu-labeled GLCL (64Cu-GLCL) was applied to an instant thin-layer chromatography medium with silica gel (iTLC-SG), and chromatography was performed using 0.1 M citric acid as the mobile phase. Measurements were taken at 0, 2, and 24 h.

sec.title: In Vivo PET Imaging-Based Biodistribution Analysis of 64Cu-GLCL
sec.p: In vivo PET imaging was performed using KPCY 7160c5 tumor model mice (n = 3). 64Cu-GLCL (200 μL, approximately 450 μCi) was administered via intravenous injection. Biodistribution images of 64Cu-GLCL in major organs (heart, liver, spleen, and muscle), along with tumor-targeting data, were obtained using a Sim PET/MRI scanner, a dedicated imaging system for small animals, at different time points (0, 2, 12, and 24 h) postinjection. The tumor-to-organ ratios (heart, liver, spleen, and muscle) and blood time-activity curves (TACs) were calculated based on %ID/g values at each time point. Quantitative analysis of the PET images was conducted using region of interest (ROI) values obtained with MIM software.

sec.title: In Vivo Therapeutic Efficacy and Safety Evaluation of GLCL
sec.p: For therapeutic experiments, NS, FG, GLL, and GLCL were intravenously administered to KPCY 7160c5-bearing mice (n = 5) every other day. All gemcitabine-containing groups (FG, GLL, GLCL) were administered at an identical gemcitabine dose of 6.75 mg/kg. Tumor size and body weight were monitored every other day throughout the treatment period. The treatment was carried out over a total period of 20 days. The overall treatment schedule and experimental design are illustrated in Figure a. Tumor volume was calculated using the following formula: V=43π(L2)(W2)(D2) where L, W, and D represent tumor length, width, and depth, respectively. The growth inhibition rate was calculated using the following formula: growth inhibition rate=1−(V̅treated,d20V̅control,d20)×100% where V̅ treated,d20 and V̅ control,d20 are the mean volumes of treated and control tumors on day 20, respectively.

On the final day of the treatment experiment, blood samples were collected via retro-orbital bleeding from all treated and control mice to compare and assess hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity. All tumor tissues and major organs (liver, spleen, kidneys, lungs, heart) were excised, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA), and paraffin-embedded. Tissue sections were stained with H&E staining to evaluate tissue damage. Tumor sections were additionally stained with Masson’s trichrome (MT) staining to assess intratumoral collagen deposition. To quantitatively evaluate intratumoral fibrosis, MT–stained sections were subjected to digital image analysis using Fiji software (ImageJ, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA). Because default stain vector settings may not optimally reflect variations in staining conditions, collagen signals were separated using the Color Deconvolution plugin with user-defined optical density vectors (“From ROI” method). Briefly, representative regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to collagen (blue), cytoplasm/muscle (red), and background (white) were manually selected from original RGB images to calibrate the deconvolution matrix. The isolated collagen channel was converted to 8-bit grayscale images, and a fixed threshold range of 0–180 (0–255 scale) was applied uniformly across all samples to segment collagen fibers. Fibrotic burden was calculated as the percentage of collagen-positive area relative to the total tissue area (% area).
